title: Compact smooth approximation of Schwartz derivatives in L2
statement: Use $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field] and Lebesgue measure on Euclidean $\mathbf R^m$, where $m\geq1$. Write $\mathcal S$ for the complex Schwartz class: smooth functions $\psi$ such that $\sup_x\|x\|^k\|D^n\psi(x)\|<\infty$ for every pair of integers $k,n\geq0$. For a multi-index $\beta\in\mathbf N^m$, put $|\beta|=\sum_j\beta_j$ and $\partial^\beta=\prod_j\partial_{x_j}^{\beta_j}$. For every $\psi\in\mathcal S$ and integer $s\geq0$, there is a sequence of smooth compactly supported complex functions $\psi_n$ such that, for every $|\beta|\leq s$, $$\|\partial^\beta\psi_n-\partial^\beta\psi\|_2\longrightarrow0.$$ Here $\|f\|_2=(\int|f(x)|^2\,dx)^{1/2}$, and all derivatives in the displayed expression are square-integrable.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2, the weak-derivative Sobolev setup before (2.1), printed p.289. Agent-stated compact-cutoff approximation prerequisite, not a separately numbered assertion of that source.

proof.text: Choose a real smooth cutoff $\chi$ with $0\leq\chi\leq1$, equal to $1$ on $\overline B(0,1)$ and with compact support $\overline B(0,2)$, using [lem-sfb-euclidean-smooth-ball-bump]. Regard it as complex-valued. By [lem-sfb-schwartz-test-inclusion-integrability] it is Schwartz. Repeatedly apply the coordinate-derivative clause of [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus]: every $\partial^\gamma\chi$ is Schwartz, and its defining bound with weight zero supplies a finite $B_\gamma\geq0$ such that $|\partial^\gamma\chi(y)|\leq B_\gamma$ for all $y$. Also every $\partial^\delta\psi$ is Schwartz and square-integrable, by the same coordinate-calculus node.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2 weak-derivative Sobolev setup before (2.1), printed p.289. The following compact-cutoff proof is supplied by the agent, not attributed to a numbered assertion in Demailly.

proof.text: For $n\in\mathbf N$ set $R_n=n+1$, $\chi_n(x)=\chi(x/R_n)$ and $\psi_n(x)=\chi_n(x)\psi(x)$. These functions are smooth by composition with a linear dilation and multiplication. Their supports are contained in $R_n\operatorname{supp}(\chi)$: if $x/R_n$ is outside the support, $\chi_n$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $x$. The dilation image of the compact support is compact, and the support of the product is closed in that image. Thus $\psi_n$ is a smooth compactly supported complex function. By [lem-sfb-schwartz-test-inclusion-integrability] it is Schwartz, and iteration of [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus] shows that every $\partial^\beta\psi_n$ is square-integrable.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2 weak-derivative Sobolev setup before (2.1), printed p.289. The following compact-cutoff proof is supplied by the agent, not attributed to a numbered assertion in Demailly.

proof.text: For a multi-index $\beta$, write $\gamma\leq\beta$ coordinatewise and $\binom\beta\gamma=\prod_j\binom{\beta_j}{\gamma_j}$. Repeated first-order chain and product rules give $$\partial^\gamma\chi_n(x)=R_n^{-|\gamma|}(\partial^\gamma\chi)(x/R_n),\qquad \partial^\beta\psi_n=\sum_{\gamma\leq\beta}\binom\beta\gamma(\partial^\gamma\chi_n)\partial^{\beta-\gamma}\psi.$$ Here is the induction: the formulas at order zero are their definitions. Applying $\partial_{x_j}$ to the first formula introduces one factor $R_n^{-1}$. Applying it to each product in the second formula differentiates either factor; reindex the first contributions by $\gamma+e_j$ and combine them with the second contributions using $\binom{b}{c-1}+\binom{b}{c}=\binom{b+1}{c}$. This proves the formulas at the next order; all functions are smooth, so the coordinate derivatives commute.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2 weak-derivative Sobolev setup before (2.1), printed p.289. The following compact-cutoff proof is supplied by the agent, not attributed to a numbered assertion in Demailly.

proof.text: Fix $|\beta|\leq s$ and put $E_{n,\beta}=\partial^\beta\psi_n-\partial^\beta\psi$. The expansion gives $$E_{n,\beta}=(\chi_n-1)\partial^\beta\psi+\sum_{0<\gamma\leq\beta}\binom\beta\gamma R_n^{-|\gamma|}(\partial^\gamma\chi)(x/R_n)\partial^{\beta-\gamma}\psi.$$ For fixed $x$, eventually $\|x\|<R_n$. Then $\chi_n$ equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $x$, and every positive-order derivative of $\chi_n$ vanishes there, so $E_{n,\beta}(x)=0$. Consequently $|E_{n,\beta}(x)|^2\to0$ for every $x$. The difference is square-integrable since $|a-b|^2\leq2|a|^2+2|b|^2$ and both derivatives are square-integrable by the preceding steps.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2 weak-derivative Sobolev setup before (2.1), printed p.289. The following compact-cutoff proof is supplied by the agent, not attributed to a numbered assertion in Demailly.

proof.text: Put $I_\beta=\{\gamma:\gamma\leq\beta\}$, $q_\beta=|I_\beta|\geq1$, $A_0=1$ and $A_\gamma=\binom\beta\gamma B_\gamma$ for $\gamma>0$. Since $R_n\geq1$ and $|\chi_n-1|\leq1$, the expansion and the finite-sum inequality $|\sum_{j=1}^q z_j|^2\leq q\sum_{j=1}^q|z_j|^2$ imply $$|E_{n,\beta}(x)|^2\leq G_\beta(x):=q_\beta\sum_{\gamma\leq\beta} A_\gamma^2|\partial^{\beta-\gamma}\psi(x)|^2.$$ Each squared derivative is integrable by repeated application of [lem-sfb-schwartz-l2-coordinate-calculus]. Thus $G_\beta$ is integrable, being a finite nonnegative linear combination of these integrable functions. It is independent of $n$. All squared errors are continuous, hence Lebesgue measurable.

source.place: WANTED locally; VI §2 weak-derivative Sobolev setup before (2.1), printed p.289. The following compact-cutoff proof is supplied by the agent, not attributed to a numbered assertion in Demailly.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-real-dominated-integral-convergence] with $F_n=|E_{n,\beta}|^2$, $f=0$ and $g=G_\beta$. The previous two steps verify measurability, integrable domination and pointwise convergence on all of $\mathbf R^m$; in particular they verify the required almost-everywhere hypotheses. It follows that $\int|E_{n,\beta}|^2\to0$. Taking square roots gives the required $L^2$ convergence: for any $\varepsilon>0$, the integral is eventually less than $\varepsilon^2$. The same sequence $\psi_n$ was defined before $\beta$ was chosen and therefore works for every $|\beta|\leq s$, including $\beta=0$ when $s=0$.
